title: AstraZeneca and Bristol Myers Squibb in Talks on $400 Billion Pharma Megadeal
excerpt: The potential tie-up would create one of the world's largest pharmaceutical companies, combining AstraZeneca's oncology dominance with Bristol Myers' immunology portfolio.
body:
• AstraZeneca and Bristol Myers Squibb have held merger talks in recent months that could create a nearly $400 billion pharma giant, the Financial Times reported
  • A deal could materialise soon but may also be delayed or fall apart, with neither company confirming discussions
  • The combination would unite AstraZeneca's fast-growing oncology franchise with Bristol Myers' strength in immunology and cardiovascular drugs

UK drugmaker AstraZeneca has been exploring a deal to combine with American rival Bristol Myers Squibb, the Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing people familiar with the matter. The potential tie-up would create one of the world's biggest pharmaceutical groups with a combined market value of nearly $400 billion.

The two companies have held talks on a potential merger in recent months, according to the FT, which added that a deal could materialise soon but could also be delayed or collapse entirely. AstraZeneca declined to comment, while Bristol Myers did not respond to requests for comment outside regular business hours, Reuters reported.

Context

The reported talks mark a dramatic shift for AstraZeneca, which a dozen years ago successfully fended off a hostile takeover bid from Pfizer. Under CEO Pascal Soriot's 14-year tenure, AstraZeneca has transformed from a company losing patent protection on legacy blockbusters into a cancer-drug powerhouse. Its share price has more than quadrupled during that period, outperforming British rival GSK and the broader FTSE 100 index.

"Cancer treatments accounted for roughly $25 billion of the company's 2025 sales — nearly half the total — followed by cardiovascular, renal, and metabolism treatments worth about $12 billion."

AstraZeneca's second-quarter results last week underscored that momentum. Cancer treatments accounted for roughly $25 billion of the company's 2025 sales — nearly half the total — followed by cardiovascular, renal, and metabolism treatments worth about $12 billion. The company reported trailing 12-month revenue of $61.4 billion as of mid-2026.

Last year, AstraZeneca unveiled plans for a direct U.S. listing alongside its existing London listing, aiming to capitalise on stronger valuations in the American market. A full merger with a U.S.-listed company like Bristol Myers could serve a similar strategic purpose.

Impact

Bristol Myers Squibb, valued at roughly $133 billion, brings its own set of strengths. The New York-based company has built a formidable immunology and cardiovascular franchise around drugs like Eliquis, one of the world's best-selling blood thinners, and Opdivo, a blockbuster cancer immunotherapy. But Bristol Myers has faced investor pressure as key patents approach expiration, and its shares have significantly underperformed the broader market over the past five years.

A combination would create a pharmaceutical company with annual revenues exceeding $100 billion and deep pipelines spanning oncology, immunology, cardiovascular disease, and rare disorders. The deal logic centres on complementary therapeutic areas: AstraZeneca's strength in targeted cancer therapies and antibody-drug conjugates paired with Bristol Myers' leadership in immune checkpoint inhibitors and cell therapy.

The sheer scale of the transaction would also attract intense regulatory scrutiny. Antitrust authorities in the U.S., EU, and UK would need to assess competitive overlaps, particularly in oncology where both companies hold significant market positions.

What's Next

Markets will be watching closely when trading opens on Monday. The deal remains far from certain — pharma mega-mergers of this scale have a history of collapsing over valuation disagreements, regulatory hurdles, and board-level politics. The last comparable transaction in the sector was AbbVie's $63 billion acquisition of Allergan in 2020, though the AstraZeneca-Bristol Myers combination would dwarf that deal.

If talks progress, the structure of any agreement will be critical. Whether AstraZeneca would acquire Bristol Myers outright, pursue a merger of equals, or explore some hybrid arrangement remains unclear. Soriot's ambitions for a U.S. listing suggest the combined entity would likely be headquartered or dual-listed in the United States, positioning it to compete directly with American giants like Eli Lilly, now valued at over $1 trillion, and Johnson & Johnson at roughly $616 billion.

For now, the FT's report has set the stage for what could become the largest pharmaceutical deal in history — or another round of talks that leads nowhere.
